faq.answer: No. Conflict style, harassment, actual danger, cultural norms, trauma safety, or an unequal relationship can produce confrontation. Consent and access conditions must be examined.
faq.question: Does confrontation establish one-to-one Eight?

faq.answer: Use decisions where both people can refuse safely, retain resources, propose changes, and seek support. Influence is mutual only when neither person faces retaliation or essential loss.
faq.question: How should mutual influence be tested?

faq.answer: Accepting a clear no, preserving the other person’s access, allowing them to set the pace, and repairing prior pressure strongly weaken a possession-centered interpretation.
faq.question: Which consent event weakens a possession hypothesis?

sections.body_md: The tradition proposes that autonomy may be tested through direct impact on a close other and resistance to being shaped in return. Observe explicit agreements and actual freedom, not chemistry alone.
sections.title: Treat intense mutual influence as a tentative pattern

sections.body_md: Use similar decisions where resources are balanced versus concentrated. Record requests, refusals, access loss, retaliation, concessions, and whether both people can revise the agreement safely.
sections.title: Compare influence under equal and unequal power

sections.body_md: One-to-one instinct is used here as a traditional attention convention, not evidence about bodily mechanisms. Attraction, trauma, coercion, attachment concerns, and violence need separate qualified support.
sections.title: Keep intensity separate from physiology

sections.body_md: The proposed pattern may appear as overt confrontation, intense loyalty, testing, possessive access rules, or quiet negotiation over who influences whom. Volume does not determine the function.
sections.title: Allow challenge, devotion, or private control

sections.body_md: Financial dependence, immigration status, workplace hierarchy, disability care, harassment, abuse, custody conflict, or unsafe housing can constrain refusal. These are safety and power facts.
sections.title: Check coercion and dependence before typology

sections.body_md: Confidence should drop when a clear no is accepted without pressure, access remains intact, decisions are shared, the person allows themselves to be influenced, and repair follows excess impact.
sections.title: Look for unpunished refusal and flexible influence

sections.body_md: This subtype cannot establish intimacy capacity, compatibility, loyalty, or relationship outcomes. Instrument-specific evidence cannot prove universal subtype ontology, and consent can be withdrawn.
sections.title: Do not infer compatibility or safe intensity

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Over five days, examine one emotionally intense decision and one ordinary shared choice with the same close person.

Observable signal: Record resources held by each person, exact request, refusal, consequence, access retained, influence accepted, agreement changed, and repair completed.

Page-specific signal: Compare mutual influence when refusal is cost-free with behavior when one person controls essential access.

Alternative explanation: Check financial dependence, immigration status, care needs, workplace hierarchy, harassment, trauma safety, custody, and housing risk.

Reflection prompt: Identify the clearest unpunished refusal and use it to revise any possession or control hypothesis.

seo.description: Type Eight one-to-one is a traditional, evidence-limited hypothesis combining Type Eight autonomy with intensity, possession, mutual influence, consent, refusal, and equal power. Confrontation or strong bonding does not establish subtype because coercion, trauma safety, unequal dependence, cultural norms, relationship agreements, harassment, and real danger can produce similar behavior.
seo.title: Type Eight one-to-one: an intensity, possession, and mutual-influence hypothesis
